_about: Malady Wise idea bank: original-wording seeds for Dxtective cases, Zebritis prompts and Triviosis/Grand Rounds questions, distilled from the old site notes and fact-checked. Fictional cases only; no individual treatment advice. Puzzle-writing tasks should pick unused items and set "used": true.

clues: A 24-year-old man has had bouts of vomiting every few weeks for a year.
Between bouts he feels completely well.
His bloods, scans and gastroscopy are all normal.
He has found that long, very hot showers are the only thing that settles the nausea.
Anti-nausea injections in the ED barely help.
He has smoked cannabis every day since he was at school.
cases.teaching_point: Cyclical vomiting eased by hot showers in a long-term daily cannabis user is the classic picture, and only sustained abstinence brings lasting relief.

clues: A 52-year-old man and his flatmate both have vomiting and watery diarrhoea.
It started about 10 hours after a home-cooked dinner.
By the next morning they feel much better and want to go home.
Their second set of liver tests is far worse than the first.
The flatmate picked the mushrooms for the meal under oak trees in Canberra.
Leftover mushrooms have a greenish cap, white gills, a skirt-like ring and a cup at the base.
cases.teaching_point: Mushroom symptoms that begin 6 or more hours after a meal, followed by a deceptive 'recovery', suggest amatoxin poisoning and need urgent Poisons Information advice even when the patient looks well.

clues: A 3-year-old girl has had a fever for five days.
Paracetamol brings the temperature down, but only for a few hours.
Both eyes are red but there is no discharge.
Her lips are red and cracked and her tongue looks like a strawberry.
Her hands and feet are puffy and she has one large lump in her neck.
Two weeks later, the skin on her fingertips starts to peel.
cases.teaching_point: Five days of fever plus red eyes, mouth changes, rash, swollen extremities or a neck node in a young child needs prompt treatment to reduce the risk of coronary artery aneurysms.

clues: A 41-year-old woman has a painful sore on her shin.
It began as a small pustule after she bumped her leg.
It grew quickly into an ulcer with a purple, overhanging edge.
Antibiotics did nothing, and a surgical clean-up made it much bigger.
She has had bouts of bloody diarrhoea for years.
A biopsy shows sheets of neutrophils and no infection.
cases.teaching_point: An ulcer that worsens after debridement (pathergy) should prompt thoughts of pyoderma gangrenosum, which is often linked to inflammatory bowel disease.

clues: A 59-year-old man has struggled to reach the toilet in time for three years.
He now feels faint whenever he stands up.
His wife says he makes a strange high-pitched noise when breathing at night.
He has developed a slow, stiff walk.
Levodopa helped only a little, and not for long.
His MRI shows a cross-shaped pattern in the pons.
cases.teaching_point: Early bladder and blood pressure problems, night-time stridor and a poor levodopa response point to MSA rather than Parkinson's disease; the 'hot cross bun' sign is a classic MRI clue.

clues: A 44-year-old woman has had migraine with aura since her twenties.
She has now had two small strokes despite normal blood pressure and cholesterol.
Her mood has dropped and her memory is slipping.
Her father had strokes and dementia in his fifties.
Her MRI shows widespread white-matter changes, including the front of the temporal lobes.
Genetic testing finds a variant in the NOTCH3 gene.
cases.teaching_point: Migraine with aura, early strokes and a strong family history suggest CADASIL, an inherited disease of the brain's small blood vessels.

clues: A 63-year-old man is brought in confused after a swim in cold ocean water.
He asks the same few questions every couple of minutes.
He knows his own name and recognises his wife.
He can't remember the last few hours and can't form new memories.
The rest of his neurological examination is normal.
By evening he is back to himself, apart from a gap in his memory of the day.
cases.teaching_point: Sudden, isolated memory loss with repetitive questioning that clears within 24 hours is typical of TGA, which does not raise stroke or dementia risk.

clues: A 17-year-old boy falls asleep in class most afternoons.
He sleeps a full night but never wakes refreshed.
Sometimes he can't move for a minute after waking.
He sees vivid dream-like figures as he drifts off.
When he laughs at a joke, his knees buckle and his face goes slack.
A sleep study shows he enters REM sleep within minutes of falling asleep.
cases.teaching_point: Excessive daytime sleepiness plus brief muscle weakness triggered by emotion (cataplexy) points to narcolepsy type 1.

clues: A 26-year-old man has been losing his hearing for two years.
Both ears are now affected, and both ring.
He has had a few falls when walking in the dark.
He had a cataract removed as a teenager.
Small lumps under his skin turned out to be nerve sheath tumours.
His MRI shows a tumour on the hearing and balance nerve on each side.
cases.teaching_point: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the hallmark of NF2-related schwannomatosis, the 2022 name for neurofibromatosis type 2.

clues: A 19-year-old man says food 'goes down slowly'.
He chews for ages and drinks water with every mouthful.
He has asthma, eczema and hay fever.
Reflux tablets have made little difference.
Last week a piece of steak got stuck and he needed it removed in hospital.
Gastroscopy shows rings and long furrows along his oesophagus.
cases.teaching_point: A young person with allergies, swallowing trouble and food getting stuck needs biopsies for eosinophilic oesophagitis.

clues: A 6-month-old girl has just started solids.
Two hours after a bowl of rice cereal, she vomits again and again.
She becomes pale and floppy and is rushed to hospital.
She is treated for possible sepsis, but all cultures are clear.
The same thing happened after her first taste of rice a month ago.
Her allergy skin prick test is negative.
cases.teaching_point: Repeated vomiting 1 to 4 hours after a food, with pallor and floppiness, suggests FPIES, a non-IgE food allergy in which rice is a common trigger in Australia.

clues: A 34-year-old woman has had a heavy, dragging right leg for two months.
It started after a viral illness and a minor fall.
Her MRI of the brain and spine is normal.
Her leg strength varies a lot from one moment to the next.
When she lifts her left leg against resistance, her 'weak' right heel presses firmly down.
Her neurologist explains it as a problem with the body's software, not its hardware.
cases.teaching_point: Functional neurological disorder is diagnosed on positive examination signs such as Hoover's sign, not just by ruling everything else out, and it is real and treatable.

clues: A 52-year-old woman's fingers turn white, then blue, in the cold.
Over several years her fingers have become tight and shiny.
She has small red spots on her face and lips.
Food sometimes sticks and she has bad heartburn.
X-rays show chalky deposits under the skin of her fingertips.
Her blood test shows anticentromere antibodies.
cases.teaching_point: Raynaud's with skin tightening, telangiectasia and calcinosis points to limited systemic sclerosis, and regular screening for pulmonary hypertension matters.

clues: A 21-year-old competitive swimmer has a heavy, aching right arm.
It started after a week of extra training.
Her arm is swollen and slightly blue.
Veins stand out across her shoulder and upper chest.
She has no cancer, no clotting history and takes no hormones.
Ultrasound shows a clot in the subclavian vein where it passes the first rib.
cases.teaching_point: A clot in the arm of a young athlete after heavy overhead activity suggests venous thoracic outlet syndrome.

clues: A 30-year-old woman has migraines and is shorter than her siblings.
She was diagnosed with hearing loss and diabetes in her twenties.
She now has sudden loss of vision on one side.
Her MRI shows stroke-like lesions that don't fit any single artery.
Her blood lactate is high.
Her mother and her mother's brother also have diabetes and deafness.
cases.teaching_point: Stroke-like episodes with deafness, diabetes and short stature passed down the maternal line suggest MELAS, a mitochondrial disease.

clues: A 23-year-old man notices blurry central vision in one eye.
It doesn't hurt.
Six weeks later, his other eye goes the same way.
His optic discs look swollen, but they don't leak dye on angiography.
His mother's brother lost his sight in his twenties.
Genetic testing finds a variant in his mitochondrial DNA.
cases.teaching_point: Painless central vision loss in one eye then the other, in a young man with affected maternal relatives, suggests LHON.

clues: A 28-year-old man has sharp central chest pain.
He had a cold last week.
The pain is worse lying flat and when he breathes in.
It eases when he sits up and leans forward.
The pain spreads to the ridge of muscle along the top of his left shoulder.
His ECG shows widespread ST elevation and PR depression.
cases.teaching_point: Sharp, positional chest pain that spreads to the trapezius ridge, with widespread ST elevation and PR depression, is typical of pericarditis.

clues: A 29-year-old woman says her own voice sounds too loud in her head.
She can hear herself breathing in her right ear.
It began after she lost 12 kg.
It disappears when she lies down or puts her head between her knees.
Her hearing test is normal.
Her right eardrum moves in and out as she breathes.
cases.teaching_point: Hearing your own voice and breath loudly, relieved by lying down and often after weight loss, suggests a patulous (stuck-open) Eustachian tube.

clues: A 32-year-old man has had a dry cough and breathlessness for a year.
He has lost weight and tires quickly at work.
He has never smoked.
His chest CT shows many small nodules, mostly in the upper lungs.
For ten years he has cut and polished kitchen benchtops.
Several of his workmates have the same diagnosis.
cases.teaching_point: Engineered stone contains very high levels of silica, and Australia banned it from 1 July 2024 after a surge of silicosis in young stonemasons.

clues: A 19-year-old woman has a rash on her trunk.
It began a week ago with a single oval pink patch.
Now many smaller patches have appeared.
Each patch has a fine collar of scale.
On her back, the patches line up like the branches of a Christmas tree.
It is only mildly itchy and her doctor expects it to fade without treatment.
cases.teaching_point: A 'herald patch' followed by a Christmas-tree pattern rash is classic pityriasis rosea, which usually clears by itself within a few months.

clues: A 27-year-old woman has a bumpy red rash around her mouth.
It burns more than it itches.
She has been putting her partner's steroid cream on it.
The cream helps for a day, then the rash returns worse.
She also uses a steroid nasal spray for hay fever.
A thin rim of skin right next to her lips is clear.
cases.teaching_point: Small bumps around the mouth that spare the lip border and flare when steroid creams stop suggest periorificial dermatitis.

clues: An 18-year-old woman has had a sore throat and fever for a week.
She is more exhausted than she has ever been.
Her tonsils are swollen with a white coating.
She has tender lumps at the back of her neck.
Two days after starting amoxicillin, an itchy red rash appears all over her body.
Her blood film shows atypical lymphocytes.
cases.teaching_point: A widespread rash after amoxicillin in a young person with sore throat and swollen neck glands is a classic clue to glandular fever, and isn't necessarily a true penicillin allergy.

clues: A 10-year-old boy was exploring rock pools on the NSW coast.
He picked up a small, sandy-coloured creature to show his dad.
He felt no more than a tiny nip on his hand.
Ten minutes later his lips and tongue go numb.
He then struggles to speak, swallow and breathe.
The creature flashed bright blue rings when he picked it up.
cases.teaching_point: Blue-ringed octopus bites are often painless, but tetrodotoxin can cause rapid paralysis, and breathing support is needed until it wears off.

clues: An 8-year-old boy has bouts of severe vomiting.
Each bout starts in the early hours of the morning and lasts a day or two.
Between bouts he is completely well.
Attacks often follow excitement, such as birthdays or the night before holidays.
His mother has migraines.
All his tests are normal and every episode looks almost identical.
cases.teaching_point: Repeated, near-identical episodes of vomiting with complete wellness in between, often in families with migraine, suggest cyclic vomiting syndrome.

clues: A 17-year-old basketballer is very tall and slim.
His arm span is longer than his height.
His breastbone sticks outwards.
The lens in one of his eyes has shifted out of place.
When he grips his wrist, his thumb and little finger overlap.
An echo shows a widened aortic root.
cases.teaching_point: Tall stature with lens dislocation and a widened aortic root points to Marfan syndrome, and regular aortic monitoring has transformed life expectancy.

clues: A 61-year-old woman has episodes of hot, red facial flushing.
She also has watery diarrhoea several times a day.
Sometimes she wheezes during a flush.
Her liver is enlarged and feels lumpy.
A new murmur is heard on the right side of her heart.
Her 24-hour urine shows a high level of 5-HIAA.
cases.teaching_point: Flushing, diarrhoea and wheeze with liver deposits and right-sided heart valve disease suggest carcinoid syndrome from a neuroendocrine tumour.

clues: A 55-year-old woman has lost 10 kg without trying.
She was recently diagnosed with diabetes.
A red, blistering rash spreads around her groin and buttocks, crusts, then moves on.
Her tongue is red and smooth and the corners of her mouth are cracked.
She had a clot in her leg last month.
A scan shows a mass in the tail of her pancreas.
cases.teaching_point: A migrating, blistering rash (necrolytic migratory erythema) with weight loss, new diabetes and clots points to a glucagonoma.

clues: A 45-year-old woman has tingling feet that has spread to her hands.
She feels unsteady in the shower when she closes her eyes.
Her diabetes and B12 tests are normal.
She takes a magnesium powder for cramps, a daily energy drink and a 'stress' B complex.
Added together, the labels show a large daily dose of pyridoxine.
Her blood B6 level is very high.
cases.teaching_point: Vitamin B6 hides in many supplements and can build up to cause nerve damage, which is why the TGA is moving 50 to 200 mg daily-dose products to pharmacist-only from mid-2027.

cases.diagnosis: Symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema (SDRIFE, 'baboon syndrome')
clues: A 30-year-old man develops a rash a few hours after a dose of medicine.
He feels well and has no fever.
The rash is bright red with sharp edges.
It covers both buttocks and the inner thighs.
There are no blisters and his mouth is clear.
He had just started amoxicillin for a chest infection.
cases.teaching_point: A sharply marked, symmetrical red rash on the buttocks and groin soon after a drug is SDRIFE, nicknamed 'baboon syndrome'.

clues: A fit 35-year-old trekker has a pounding headache.
She says it feels like the worst hangover of her life.
She has no appetite and feels sick.
She barely slept in the teahouse last night.
She flew into Lukla and climbed quickly over two days.
She is now sleeping at 3,800 m.
cases.teaching_point: Headache with nausea, fatigue or poor sleep after a fast climb is acute mountain sickness, and being fit gives no protection.

clues: A 38-year-old woman can't sit through a film any more.
In the evenings she has an urge to move her legs.
Getting up and walking eases it straight away.
Her partner says her legs jerk while she sleeps.
She donates blood every few months.
Her ferritin is low at 18 micrograms per litre.
cases.teaching_point: Restless legs often reflect low iron stores, and frequent blood donors are at particular risk.

clues: A 34-year-old woman has pelvic pain that builds as her bladder fills.
Emptying her bladder brings relief.
She passes urine up to 15 times a day.
Every urine culture has been negative.
Coffee, chilli and fizzy drinks make it flare.
Cystoscopy has ruled out other causes.
cases.teaching_point: Bladder pain with frequency and repeatedly negative urine cultures suggests bladder pain syndrome, a diagnosis made after other causes are excluded.

cases.diagnosis: Chronic cough from ear wax (Arnold's ear-cough reflex)
clues: A 70-year-old man has had a dry cough for four months.
His chest X-ray and lung function tests are normal.
He doesn't take blood pressure tablets and has no reflux.
Asthma inhalers have done nothing.
He mentions his right ear has felt blocked for months.
His cough stops the week his ear is cleared.
cases.teaching_point: A branch of the vagus nerve supplies the ear canal, so wax or a foreign body in the ear can trigger a chronic cough.

clues: A 33-year-old man has painful purple patches on both ears.
Similar net-like patches appear on his cheeks and legs.
Some areas have turned black.
His white cell count is low.
His ANCA test is strongly positive.
He uses cocaine most weekends.
cases.teaching_point: Levamisole, a common cocaine cutting agent, can cause purple ear lesions, a low neutrophil count and positive ANCA.

clues: A 33-year-old woman's hair is coming out in handfuls.
Her ponytail is thinner, but there are no bald patches.
A gentle tug pulls out several hairs with tiny white bulbs.
Her scalp looks healthy.
She had a baby four months ago.
Her doctor reassures her that regrowth usually follows within months.
cases.teaching_point: Diffuse shedding 2 to 4 months after a big stressor such as childbirth, illness or surgery is telogen effluvium, and it usually recovers.

clues: A 56-year-old woman has pain on the outside of her hip.
She can't lie on that side at night.
Stairs and standing on one leg make it worse.
Pressing on the bony point of her hip is very tender.
Her hip joint itself moves freely.
Ultrasound shows a damaged gluteal tendon.
cases.teaching_point: Outer hip pain once labelled 'trochanteric bursitis' is usually a gluteal tendon problem.

clues: A 34-year-old man has a heart attack while playing squash.
He doesn't smoke and isn't overweight.
His father died of a heart attack at 46.
He has firm lumps on his Achilles tendons.
There is a pale ring around the edge of each cornea.
His LDL cholesterol is 7.2 mmol/L.
cases.teaching_point: Very high LDL with tendon xanthomas and early heart disease in the family suggests FH, which affects about 1 in 250 to 300 people, so relatives should be tested.

clues: A 41-year-old woman is diagnosed with bowel cancer.
The tumour is on the right side of her colon.
Her mother had womb cancer at 48.
Her uncle had bowel cancer at 45.
Her tumour is missing mismatch repair proteins on testing.
A blood test finds a variant in the MLH1 gene.
cases.teaching_point: Early bowel and womb cancers across generations point to Lynch syndrome, and each child of a carrier has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it.

clues: A 66-year-old woman wakes and the room spins as she rolls over.
It lasts less than a minute.
It happens again when she looks up to reach a high shelf.
She has no hearing loss or ringing.
Between episodes she feels fine.
Lying her back quickly with her head turned brings on a burst of rotating eye movements.
cases.teaching_point: Brief spinning triggered by head position, with a positive Dix-Hallpike test, is BPPV.

clues: A 28-year-old man has a routine blood test before starting a new job.
His neutrophil count is low at 1.1.
He feels well and has never had serious infections.
His blood tests over the past 10 years show the same result.
His family comes from Sudan.
Testing shows his red cells lack the Duffy antigen.
cases.teaching_point: A lower neutrophil count linked to the Duffy-null blood group is common and harmless in people of African and Middle Eastern ancestry, and recognising it avoids needless tests.

clues: A 30-year-old backpacker develops fever, headache and back pain.
It started a few days after a jungle tour in South America.
Despite a temperature of 39.8 degrees, his pulse is only 70.
He improves for a day, then turns yellow.
He starts bleeding from his gums.
He skipped one travel vaccine because 'it wasn't compulsory'.
cases.teaching_point: High fever with a slow pulse (Faget sign), a brief remission, then jaundice and bleeding suggests yellow fever, and one vaccine dose protects for life.

Roughly how many times a day does a person swallow?
What proportion of people with silent gallstones develop symptoms over 10 to 15 years?
Which type of fibre helps irritable bowel syndrome: psyllium or bran?
Does avoiding nuts, corn and seeds prevent diverticulitis flares?
trivia.a: No, there is no good evidence it helps

trivia.a: A false recovery while liver damage worsens
wrong: A rash that proves it is harmless

trivia.q: What is the recommended first aid for a bluebottle sting in Australia?
trivia.a: Hot water immersion (about 45 degrees) for 20 minutes

trivia.q: Which jellyfish sting is treated first with vinegar?
The blue-ringed octopus paralyses with which toxin?
Which fish poisoning makes cold things feel hot and hot things feel cold?

trivia.a: It reads carboxyhaemoglobin as oxygenated haemoglobin

trivia.q: Levamisole, which can cause ear purpura and low neutrophils, is a common cutting agent in which drug?
Hoover's sign tests for functional weakness by checking which movement in the 'weak' leg?
trivia.a: Involuntary hip extension when the other leg lifts

trivia.a: Sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotion, like laughter

trivia.q: Which 2009 flu vaccine was linked to a rise in narcolepsy in Europe?

wrong: Makes a stroke likely within a week
